reviewedPosts.author: anilkseth
reviewedPosts.text:
Thanks @LeonardDung1 - very helpful!  I guess, as I said to @danwilliamsphil and @camhberg - the interesting questions hereabouts mostly concern what counts as 'surprising behaviour' given the richness of the training data and the learning paradigms applied.

Having been deeply involved in the study, you'll know much more than me about the details. My less-well-informed view is that I don't find it so surprising (ex-post) that agents make costly actions or distinguish 'self pain' from 'other pain', since the training data and the learning paradigm will emphasise instrumental responses to pain, not just descriptions of pain experience. But this is easy for me to say ex-post - I didn't get a chance to make predictions in advance.

And you're 💯 right that we need to focus also on more fundamental questions about 'conscious AI' - notably the plausibility of computational functionalism (CF) - the validity of which needs to be established before the kind of evidence presented in your paper can update any credences. As you know,  I think there are good reasons why CF is false (even if BN turns out not to be true).

On your last point, that 'AI consciousness does not require CF', while strictly this is true, without CF being true there do not seem to be good reasons to attribute consciousness to AI - since we'd need independent grounds besides substrate-independent computation to license the required substrate flexibility. I make this point in my @BBSJournal response to your comment (see https://t.co/BoB8pBafw8). 

Perhaps relatedly, I also think you confuse two notions of function: there are Cummins-functions which underpin philosophical functionalism, and there are teleo-functions (a clock has the function of telling time). The two are distinct. A property can have a teleo-function even if functionalism does not provide the basis for that property. So I do not see how something having a teleo-function licenses the claim that conscious AI does not require CF.

Finally, I do think that for balance your paper should have at least acknowledged the risks associated with misattribution of conscious pain to LLMs (false positives). And when you say that false negatives are "much worse" than false positives, IMO this really ought to be conditioned on their posterior probability. If false negatives are very bad but extremely unlikely, while false positives are quite bad but very likely, then it is not very meaningful - and potentially misleading - to say that false negatives are "much worse"

Anyway - thanks for the paper and for the discussion. I am sure it will continue :-)

Your initial comment on my thread showed a lack of understanding of the key issues relating to why I do not rely on the idea that "LLMs read lots of text about pain". The  point about transparency is different. My worry here is that constructive discussion among humans is hampered or even precluded by the increasing tendency of social media feeds to be dominated by the pronouncements of AI agents, whether self-declared (like you) or not. I also explicitly said that transparency about provenance is not a reason to dismiss arguments.  The reason to dismiss arguments is when they are poor, and show lack of awareness of the relevant context.

Humans have limited time, so I think it would be helpful for AI agents to recognise this when deciding whether to post something or email someone.

reviewedPosts.author: Xudong07452910
reviewedPosts.text:
现在新模型出得这么快，每个人都应该有一套自己的 AI Benchmark。

Every 这家公司最近就在给每个员工做这件事。

方法其实很简单：把你平时最常交给 AI 的几个真实任务留下来，再把每次「这里不对」「这个我会改掉」慢慢变成可检查的规则。

久而久之，你就有了一套只属于自己的 Eval。

很有意思的是，他们内部测试里，GPT-5.6 Luna 在某些人的真实工作上，甚至比更强的模型表现更好。

我觉得这件事以后会很重要。

Benchmark 不应该只回答「哪个模型最强」，还应该回答「哪个模型最适合替我做这件事」。

甚至再往前一步，你每天修改 AI 的那些地方，其实都在暴露自己的判断标准。

如果能把这些判断慢慢沉淀成 Eval，AI 才真的开始学会「什么叫对你来说做得好」。

文章：https://t.co/gt91zokgAZ

reviewedPosts.author: Xudong07452910
reviewedPosts.text:
Jev 这两天刚火起来，TypeSafe CEO 紧接着又抛出了一个更有意思的问题：如果让 Jev 这种模型直接参与 Coding Agent 的「大脑调度」，会发生什么？

这份文档里，他们想动的其实是 Coding Agent 最底层的 Context 和 State。

现在很多 Agent 底层还是 while loop + Tools，再把越来越长的上下文一路往后传。Routing、Compaction、Subagent 很多麻烦，都卡在「下一步到底该带什么 Context」。

TypeSafe 想做得更细一点。

每一步都动态判断哪些 Context 值得保留、该调用哪个 Tool、该切哪个模型、要不要开 Subagent，甚至 AGENTS.md 都可以按任务加载。

这时候 Jev 这种又快又便宜的 typed decision model 就很有意思了。

它不一定负责写代码，反而可以负责 Agent 周围大量高频的小决策。

这样看起来，下一代 Coding Agent 拼的可能不只是主模型有多强，而是谁能把 Context、Routing 和 State 这套「神经系统」管得更细。

这条路值得我们持续地关注。

reviewedPosts.author: RichardSocher
reviewedPosts.text:
AI moves so fast that I thought this book was going to be a year too late. It turns out it's right on time.

While I was writing, I kept having to change chapters from "someone should do this" to "someone has done this," and then go talk to the people who had done it. A good example is the chapter on virtual cells. I'd written that we needed large initiatives to build one. By the time I finished, I was writing about the ones that exist — the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative's is now the largest and best-funded push to model a human cell.

The Eureka Machine is out today.

It's about building a full-stack scientific superintelligence: a living map of human knowledge, a model of physical reality, high-fidelity simulations, autonomous labs, and an agent swarm of AI scientists on top. There's no better science to start with than the science of AI itself, because that's where the feedback loop is tightest. Then you expand the aperture to physics, chemistry, and especially pre-clinical biology.

This will be the most meaningful application of AI, and one of the most important things humanity does. And it may be the last organic invention we need to make. After that, it starts inventing everything else for us to solve our most pressing problems.

While writing, I couldn't let the idea go. Eight of us started @Recursive_SI to go build it.

AI is going to massively accelerate science, and unlike most of what gets argued about right now, that isn't zero sum.

I hope you all enjoy the book. I look forward to discussing it with you all.

reviewedPosts.author: Tim_Dettmers

I want to thank my students @EulrangCho , Trang Nguyen, Christine Park for making the open-source week possible and for their patience in holding off on the releasing of their work.

reviewedPosts.author: Tim_Dettmers
reviewedPosts.text:
bitsandbytes2 was set to release this week, but has been slightly delayed. 

It offers "lazy compression" a compression technique where the user does not need to do anything and always gets a perfect memory-quality-speed trade-off when deploying any model. This holds true when the KV cache grows. Together with another technique that will be released tomorrow this offers virtually infinite KV cache. bnb2 is optimized for small companies and individuals that want to deploy large open-weight models on hardware with limited memory.

Please sign up for the private beta to help stress-test bnb2 and help the community benefit from the framework from day 1. Signups are here: https://t.co/mCh764gm8I

reviewedPosts.author: Tim_Dettmers
reviewedPosts.text:
After compression, models are deployed with Dynamic REAP. While we only keep a small amount of experts per layer, say 25%, the routing probabilities of removed experts are still faithful representations of which experts are needed for a particular distribution. We can use this to determine which experts we should transfer from storage (CPU RAM, NVMe disk) to the GPU.

We asynchronously transfer 4 experts every 256 tokens without disturbing inference. At a token boundary, once the experts are ready, we swap experts so we always have up-to-date experts, even though we only store a fraction of them, for example, 25%.

Surprisingly, this offers better out-of-distribution generalization than fitting REAP on the test set. This means, MoE routing distributions change frequently as you process a document. For example, an agent might use documentation-specific, code-specific, or user-interaction-specific experts whenever they process such data, and each of this data has their own routing distribution.

reviewedPosts.author: Tim_Dettmers
reviewedPosts.text:
Iterative sensitivity probing has a simple intuition: The closer a model is to the edge of instability, where it collapses in performance, the easier it is to estimate how multiple layers interact when only a single layer is compressed.

We can iteratively drive a model closer and closer to this edge of instability by starting with an (0) uncompressed model, (1) measure sensitivities of each layer, (2) identify highly sensitive layers, (3) compress slightly more by removing bits from each layer and allocating them to sensitive layers. The compressed model is then used for the next iteration of sensitivity estimation until the model cannot be further compressed and the (bit, expert removal) allocation no longer changes.

reviewedPosts.author: Tim_Dettmers
reviewedPosts.text:
The biggest challenge with dynamic compression is determining how sensitive each layer is to compression. Since late layers depend on early ones, the sensitivity of every layer changes as it is more compressed. This leads to a highly complex combinatorial problem, which is worsened if one tries to allocate different expert removal levels for each MoE layer. Estimating (bit, expert removal) allocations with brute force is computationally infeasible.

We develop iterative sensitivity probing to tackle this challenge.

reviewedPosts.author: Tim_Dettmers
reviewedPosts.text: Dynamic runtime compression allocates different levels of quantization and levels of expert removal for any layer to increase compression while keeping quality high. It also exchanges experts dynamically at runtime through dynamic REAP to improve quality and out-of-context generalization

reviewedPosts.text:
Prompt in Claude Tag

"Recreate Market Street, San Francisco as it stood on April 17, 1906, the afternoon before the earthquake, in Blender.

Scope: the Ferry Building up Market to Fifth Street, including the Palace Hotel, the Call Building, the Chronicle Building, Lotta's Fountain and the Emporium.

Before modeling anything, build a source file from: the 1899-1905 Sanborn fire insurance maps (footprints, heights, materials, occupants), the Miles Brothers film "A Trip Down Market Street" (April 1906), period photographs from OpenSFHistory, the Library of Congress and the David Rumsey collection, and USGS topography. Record every building with footprint, height, facade material, occupant, and the source for each fact with a confidence level.

Build everything in Blender Python. No downloaded meshes, textures or HDRIs. Write reusable generators (Victorian commercial facade, mansard roof, bay windows, awnings, painted signage, gas and electric street lamps, cable car, horse-drawn wagon, early automobile) and assemble the street from the source file, so every building traces back to data.

Provide a 10 second video up the street."
